country.comment: Study conducted across three neighbourhoods (City Bowl, Mitchells Plain, and Dunoon) in Cape Town, South Africa.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF p. 3, Fig. 1; PDF p. 5, Participant selection and data collection

effect_estimate.comment: Mixed-methods Q-methodology study reporting factor loadings, explained variance, and ideal Q-sort scores rather than a causal regression effect estimate of tariffs on physical access.
effect_estimate.value: Principal component analysis with varimax rotation of 27 usable Q-sorts (across 25 tariff-fairness statements) identified five distinct perspectives on which 24 of 27 Q-sorts loaded significantly (factor loading threshold ±0.516 at p < 0.01), explaining 61% of sample variance: Factor 1 'the Insurer' (15% variance, n = 6 Q-sorts), Factor 2 'the Individualist' (11% variance, n = 4 Q-sorts, all in working-class Mitchells Plain with high monthly water bills), Factor 3 'the Bureaucrat' (15% variance, n = 7 Q-sorts, 6 of 7 in affluent City Bowl), Factor 4 'the Humanitarian' (11% variance, n = 4 Q-sorts, all in low-income/informal Dunoon), and Factor 5 'the Prepper' (9% variance, n = 3 Q-sorts). All five factors rejected volume-independent flat rates (Statement 17 ideal scores -3 to -4; consensus at P < 0.05) and four of five supported pro-poor tariff redistribution/free basic water, whereas 'the Individualist' (Mitchells Plain households facing the highest monthly bills due to larger household sizes than City Bowl and incomes above free-water eligibility) opposed free basic water (Statement 10: 0, P < 0.01) and favoured prepaid options (Statement 14: +2, P < 0.01) and citizen participation in tariff-setting (Statement 4: +4, P < 0.01), while 'the Humanitarian' (Dunoon residents where mandatory water management devices and indigent registration fostered mistrust) strongly supported free basic water (+3) and minimising financial burdens on poor households.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 6–10, Table 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Analysis and interpretation, and Results

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <= 2 by the MMAT study design ceiling. Assigned 1 because the primary empirical study documents factor-analytic and descriptive associations among neighbourhood socioeconomic context, household size/income, self-reported monthly water bills (Fig. 3), and subjective perceptions of tariff fairness, while relying on secondary literature and plausible inference rather than direct empirical observation of indigent registration decisions or WMD supply cutoffs within the sampled households.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 4, Past and present patterns of injustice; PDF pp. 7–11, Fig. 3, Results, and Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines block tariffs, fixed charges, cost recovery, and prepaid water options (fees); indigent free basic water and pensioner rebates (hardship_exception) conditioned on proving and registering indigent status (procedural_steps) and mandatory installation of supply-limiting water management devices or prepaid cutoffs (disconnection); citizen participation in setting tariffs (participation); and property-value-based tariff differentiation and backyarder housing dynamics (property).

mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4, Past and present patterns of injustice; PDF p. 6, Table 1; PDF pp. 7–12, Results and Discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Primary empirical analysis compares household monthly water costs against household income and size across the three neighbourhoods (affordability, Fig. 3) and records household running water access in home/yard while evaluating perspectives on free basic water and extending access to underserved neighbourhoods (water_access, Table 1 Statements 10 and 18). Supply cutoffs via WMDs and uninterrupted supply preferences are also discussed contextually.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Q-methodology explicitly combines quantitative principal component analysis with varimax rotation and significance testing of 27 structured Q-sorts (plus descriptive comparison of household income, size, and water bills) with qualitative key-informant statement generation, individual interviews, and crib-sheet narrative interpretation.

sample_size.comment: 30 residents were interviewed individually via convenience and snowball sampling across three Cape Town areas, producing 27 usable Q-sorts (24 of which loaded significantly on the five retained factors at p < 0.01); statement concourse winnowed from ~40 piloted statements to 25 final statements.
sample_size.value: 30 respondents interviewed, yielding 27 usable Q-sorts (8 in Dunoon, 8 in Mitchells Plain, 11 in City Bowl) sorting 25 statements
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 5, Statements for the Q-sorts and Participant selection and data collection; PDF p. 7, Analysis and interpretation

study_design.comment: Authors explicitly characterise Q method as combining quantitative factor analysis (PCA with varimax rotation in PQMethod on 27 Q-sorts of 25 statements) and qualitative crib-sheet discourse analysis of subjective viewpoints across three purposively contrasted neighbourhoods, using convenience and snowball sampling.
study_design.value: Q-methodology study (mixed quantitative principal component analysis with varimax rotation and qualitative crib-sheet discourse interpretation of individual Q-sort interviews)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF pp. 4–7, Methodology
